opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's actually a really interesting dynamic to watch. Roughly, the way I see it right now is that the closed frontier models are ahead, and the open-source models are trailing behind by some amount of time. Maybe it's something like six months to a year, depending on how you measure it and which capability you care about. And that gap has been surprisingly stable, or even shrinking, in some areas.

I think it ends up looking a bit like the operating system ecosystem. You have a few closed platforms, like Windows and macOS, and then you have Linux, which is open and lags in some ways but is incredibly important and ends up running a huge amount of the world. I can see something similar happening with LLMs: a small number of closed frontier labs pushing the absolute edge, and then an open ecosystem that's a bit behind but is very healthy, very hackable, and gets used for an enormous number of things.

What I find exciting about the open side is that it's not just about matching benchmark numbers. A lot of the value is that people can actually get in there, fine-tune, distill, run things locally, inspect the weights, and build on top of it in ways that just aren't possible with an API. That's where a lot of the creativity and experimentation comes from, and a lot of the research too, because academics and small teams can't really do science on a model they can't touch.

Now, the frontier is still very expensive. Training the very best models takes huge amounts of compute, data work, and infrastructure, so I don't think open source magically catches up at the very top just because people want it to. But for a lot of use cases you don't need the absolute best model. You need something that's good enough, cheap, private, and that you control. As capabilities improve across the board, "good enough" covers more and more ground, and I think open models eat a lot of that.

So I don't see it as a winner-take-all thing. I'd actually be a little worried if everything was locked up in a couple of closed systems. I think it's healthier for the ecosystem to have a strong open counterweight, and I'm hopeful that's the way it plays out.

r001.rationale: It says training the very best models takes huge amounts of compute, data work, and infrastructure, identifying capital-intensive requirements as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: It says open models suit “a lot of use cases” that do not need the absolute best model, but does not say they are adequate for the vast majority of consumer use cases.

r003.rationale: It mentions running models locally and predicts that “good enough” will cover more ground, but does not clearly predict locally run models will cover a large share of simple AI use cases.

r004.rationale: It says frontier models will remain expensive and that many use cases do not need the best model, but does not suggest frontier intelligence will be needed only for work at Nobel Prize research level.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that there's basically a gap, and the question is what's happening to the gap over time, and also what's happening to the absolute level of the open models.

So historically, the frontier labs are ahead, and then the open ecosystem is maybe a year or so behind, roughly, depending on how you measure it. And I actually think that's a pretty stable dynamic for a while. The frontier labs have a few things going for them. They have the compute, obviously, but more importantly I think they have the data, especially the proprietary data they've collected through deployment, the RLHF data, all the human feedback, all the stuff that's really hard to replicate from the outside. And they have the people and the infrastructure and the know-how, a lot of which is sort of tacit knowledge that doesn't make it into papers anymore.

But the thing that's interesting is that the open models don't need to be at the frontier to be extremely useful. For a huge fraction of what people actually want to do, you don't need the absolute best model. You need a model that's good enough, that you can run yourself, that you can fine-tune, that you can inspect, that doesn't phone home, that you control. And the "good enough" bar is now being cleared by open models for a very large set of tasks. So in some sense the open models are competing less on "are we the smartest" and more on being this kind of substrate that everyone can build on. It's a little bit like Linux. Linux didn't win by being the fanciest operating system. It won by being there and being free and being hackable.

The other thing I'd say is that I think a lot of the value is going to move toward smaller models anyway. I've been kind of obsessed with this idea that the current frontier models are actually bloated. They've memorized a huge amount of the internet that is just not that useful for the core cognitive stuff, and I think we're going to see much smaller models that distill the reasoning core and look up facts when they need them. And that regime is very favorable to the open ecosystem, because training a really good small model is much more accessible than training a trillion-parameter model. The barrier to entry is just a lot lower.

Where I'd be a bit more cautious is on the very frontier. The hardest, most agentic, long-horizon stuff, I think the closed labs will probably keep a lead there, because that's exactly where the proprietary data and the enormous compute and the deployment flywheel matter the most. And if you believe the frontier is where a lot of the economic value concentrates, then that lead is meaningful.

So I guess my overall picture is, the open models are not going to be at the frontier most of the time, but they're going to be close enough, and they're going to be the default for a very large fraction of actual usage, and I think that's actually a pretty healthy equilibrium. I'd be much more worried about a world where there was no strong open alternative at all.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier labs have more compute and that training trillion-parameter models has a high barrier to entry, identifying resource intensity as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: It says open models now clear the “good enough” bar for a very large set of tasks people want to do.

r003.rationale: It predicts open models will become the default for a very large fraction of actual usage and notes that users can run them themselves.

r004.rationale: It describes frontier work as hard, agentic, and long-horizon, but does not say frontier intelligence will be needed mainly for work at the level of Nobel Prize research.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is how much capability you actually need for a particular application. There are tasks where you really want the strongest model available, and you’re willing to pay for it. But a huge number of tasks don’t require that. You need a model that does one thing reliably, cheaply, and with acceptable latency.

So as open models improve, more applications cross that threshold. And then the ability to run the model yourself, customize it, keep your data local—those become pretty compelling advantages. You don’t necessarily need to win on every benchmark to be extremely useful.

The frontier is also moving, though. Better models let people attempt things they wouldn’t have tried before, so there’s this expanding set of problems where the extra intelligence matters. I’d expect both to coexist: open models handling a lot of practical workloads, and frontier models pushing into tasks that are still just barely possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses cost and practical advantages but does not identify capital intensity as an obstacle to open models competing with frontier models.

r002.rationale: It says many tasks do not need the strongest model, but does not state that current open-source models are adequate for most consumer use cases.

r003.rationale: It says more applications may become suitable for open models and mentions running models yourself, but does not clearly predict that locally run models will cover a large share of simple AI use cases.

r004.rationale: The response does not suggest that frontier intelligence will be needed mainly for work at the level of Nobel Prize research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a question of how much intelligence you actually need for a particular application. You don’t necessarily need the best model in the world to do something useful. As open models get better, more applications cross that threshold where you can run them yourself, customize them, and have control over the data and the deployment.

The frontier models can still be incredibly valuable for the hardest problems. If a model is a little bit better at research or coding, that difference can matter a lot. So I don’t think there’s necessarily one winner. You could have a small number of frontier models pushing the capabilities forward, and then a very broad ecosystem of open models doing a huge amount of the actual work.

The thing I’d watch is the gap between them, and how quickly the requirements of applications move. Do people settle into tasks that open models can handle, or does every improvement create demand for the next level of intelligence? I suspect we’ll see both.

r001.rationale: The response discusses model capability gaps and deployment control, but does not identify capital intensity as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: It says open models can handle more applications as they improve, but does not state that current open-source models are adequate for the vast majority of consumer use cases.

r003.rationale: It describes more applications crossing the threshold for self-hosting, but does not predict that locally run models will cover a large share of simple AI use cases.

r004.rationale: It mentions frontier models remaining valuable for the hardest research and coding problems, but does not suggest their need will be concentrated in work at the level of Nobel Prize research.
